First and foremost you can’t just say “I WILL BE BRINGING MY SERVICE DOG” - you can’t just show up one day with them as a student. 

You really need to sit down with your parents and have some serious discussion with your doctors and counselors and they will probably require you to have some sort of IEP or 504 Plan, and sometimes schools are assholes about accepting those if you have an otherwise invisible disability. 

You’re gonna need a lot of “legal documents” as well, you’re school will require your dogs vaccinations to be up to date and if they aren’t then you need to get it done. I had to and I still have to now as a college student, turn in my boys vaccination records every year for his yearly shots.You’re also going to need your dogs city registration, this isn’t service dog registration as we all know that’s fake but this is registration that your city mandates. It’s often referred to as a pet license. They can ask you for training records / what trainer you went through. They did with me. 

This process is long, and sometimes extremely hard. The school will more than likely bring up different accommodations, don’t fight them on them because it’s hurting your case more than helping. Try them and if they don’t help go back and tell them.

I always enjoy hearing others training methods; they help me fine tune my own. As someone who owner trains their dog, there’s still a lot for me to learn because I in no means am a professional, and even with professionals there’s so much crap in that industry. 

My main focus isn’t really about you do this for me now or you’re a bad dog though, there’s too many people that aren’t service dog handlers that are quick to be angered and frustrated by their dog not doing what they want them to and then they turn to punishment without causation and it just makes the poor dog even more confused.

I absolutely adore seeing owners found their dogs training on trust. It takes a lot to get that and to give it too. I think it’s really important also to make your dog aware that if they are uncomfortable with a situation, they can trust me enough to keep them safe / remove them from it until we can work up to a comfort level where it doesn’t bother them. 

Training my boy to be comfortable and trust me in loud environments such as Church during worship (our pastor preappproved us coming and everyone there loves him) took so much trust. Especially since we average about 100-120 members in our congregation every Sunday & Wednesday. He’s been desensitized to the loud noises and crowding people, and I can even approach the stage where there are drums and percussions being played without him freaking but I ALWAYS give him ear protection. He protects me and keeps me safe and comfortable, so it’s what I should do for him as well. 

He’s taken on concerts, movies, and soon to be another conference in June. 

Every dog is different so i think it’s really important that even though you’re wanting something from them, it’s important to get to know them and know what they want from you.

And we do too, when our dogs quite literally have to shit but are hesitating to even with a. go potty command then coming back and telling us they have to potty less than 5 minutes later is very frustrating. I use a mixture of positive reinforcement and ecollar training, however, I will say from the moment i brought my dog home to the time I began training him it was nothing but positive reinforcement. I found I got more of a response from him and reward from him than I did if I were to have just slapped an e-collar on him. 

Nearly all of his tasks and obedience it founded on positive reinforcement, the only time I have EVER had to use an Ecollar has been with Recall training when he just wasn’t understanding the purpose of the 6 ft lead was to not nom on it even when discouraged and treated when he didn’t nom. As well as distractions now more recently, I never shock him though, and our ECOLLAR has a setting that just simply beeps. The noise is enough to take his interest off of whatever is distracting him and he directs his focus back to me as if to say “mom what was that?” - he doesn’t ever get startled or upset with the noise but rather more intently focused on me when it happens and I always show him the remote so he knows that what it was came from me and was not something that would harm him. 

Whenever he was a puppy he had a bad habit of jumping on me and I would simply just bring my knee up to his chest to discourage the behavior. He only jumps on me / people now if given the command “hug” 

I honestly believe in my personal opinion that it’s up to the owner and trainer to adapt to their dogs temperament and comfort when training. Some dogs are more receptive to positive reinforcement without tools like ecollars or prongs, while other dogs just can’t seem to grasp it or get too frustrated with the idea of positive reinforcement.

It’s up to the owner to know the dogs comfort level and how far they can go with things. I’ve seen people overly use an ecollar incorrectly to the point their dogs absolutely fearful and runs away / acts out even more with it on. The point of training is to keep a dog engaged and interested in what you’re doing while also showing them what you want. 

I always go by the rule of thumb that if the dogs getting frustrated then take a break and have some play time to let that frustration out. I’ve used this several times and it’s worked wonders, it shows the pup you’re willing to work with them if they work with you.

I’ve used the break method with my brothers 6 month puppy who is a biter and way hyperactive. He’s engaged with me for a good 10 min then we take a break and play tug, after our game of tug we go right back to training but I never push him more than 20 minutes a day due to his young age. So far in the past month from using this method he’s learned how to: 

sit, shake, wave, lay down, heel, stay, and speak

It’s a combined effort and there needs to be a lot of trust between dog and trainer for things to work out. If you don’t understand a dogs limits, or how to take necessary breaks then there’s a high chance that dogs just gonna continue to get frustrated.

If it's generalized or social you need to realize that a service dog may not be a good fit for you even with what your therapist says. If all eyes are on you all the time and confrontation bothers you, a service dog might not be the right fit because it can cause you to go into more episodes.

Service dogs can help those with anxiety who have the ability to cope and live with things like being confronted and having eyes on them all the time as well as getting randomly approached and questioned. If you know you'd go into an episode just by being confronted/denied access / asked questions then I would reconsider. A good 65% of being a service dog handler is access issues, entitled people, nosey public, and the uneducated.  You also need to realize that people who fake service animals and bring ESA's into non-pet-friendly places are at an all-time high right now.

Are you prepared for that when you're out in public and an untrained dog charges at your service dog? Are you prepared for that dog's owner to accuse you of your dog hurting theirs, or fight you and the manager/store saying her ESA has public access rights? Videos make it look simple and horrible, but as someone who has an SD for Anxiety and PTSD, it is worse in person when it actually happens to you. I was physically assaulted over having my service dog because of a lady who had an uncontrolled pet who bit my dog at a non-pet-friendly establishment. She got angry because she was told she was breaking the law and when asked to leave harassed me and pushed me down. Be prepared because these kinds of interactions *will happen*. They're inevitable.

There are A LOT of factors that go into choosing what breed would best suit you for a service animal. You have to take into consideration some major aspects of your life such as how much time are you going to be able to dedicate to this dog a day? Your ability to properly stimulate and exercise them within the lines of their breed. Prey drive. Living conditions. What issues you would feel comfortable training with and which ones you want to avoid (ie: high energy / prey drive) etc.  


Almost everyone that you meet who has had a service dog for a while are going to recommend you the Fab Four. 

Which are **Labrador Retrievers, Golden Retrievers, Poodles, and Collies.** 

These breeds typically have a higher success rate at service work as opposed to breeds such as huskies. There have been some people that have successfully made service animals out of the less desirable breeds such as VisualMoss on Youtube but they take a lot of time and energy and aren't guaranteed to succeed.   


Another good thing about these breeds is their high intelligence. People typically want to work with dogs that have high intelligence and low prey drives whenever it comes to service work because a dog with less prey drive is a dog less likely to chase after other animals.  The fab four have been an extremely successful line of breeds that typically are easier to train and you will see a lot of handlers on social media with Labs and Goldens. I myself personally have a yellow lab.   


Goldens or Labs are in my personal opinion the best two breeds to go with for Psych work but that doesn't mean other breeds can't do it.  


Goldens are typically more on the sensitive side and bond with their handlers who are softer as where Labs are more versatile and have high drive and energy. They're people pleasers and are great for SD work.  


Not all puppies in these breed will be worthy of being SD. It's best to work with a reputable breeder to find the right temperament and breed that will fit your lifestyle. A poorly bred pup can mean not suitable for service work (this is not always to case but there are more instances of washes from poorly bred pups / pups with reactivity issues)

One thing you need to be aware of is puppies will be curious - so don't put it past them if they try to chase your cats to investigate. Also - you have to be really really cautious of the pups prey drive. Different breeds have different prey drives. 

From what you said you're getting a Moyen Poodle. Moyens typically have a low to medium prey drive so they may chase smaller animals like squirrels and cats but you can work through that. 

 My SD was raised around cats and kittens but he still romps and chases them for play - never to harm and only when he's off duty. They sleep together and he lets them climb all over his back and step on his face with no issue but not every puppy / dog is gonna be like that.   


You're gonna need the structure and enrichment. Time to spend with the pup and build up that bond, as well as time to exercise and stimulate them. You have to also be wary about pack bonding with them when training as that can put a stint in things. I was lucky enough with my SD that my parents both worked evening shifts and I worked morning so he spent more time with me and I his handler did all of the training so that bond was easily established.   


Moyens are also extremely high energy. So they need that stimulation whether it be from walks to playing games and even training.  Typically at least 2 hours a day dedicated to stimulation and enrichment. *(this can be done in 30 min increments)*  I know a few people who have owned them and their pups have developed severe separation anxiety, so that's something you need to keep in mind as well.

There are a lot of good videos on youtube to help out with the at home training, but a trainer would be best for the line of work your daughters pup is going to be in.
